sections.normalized_html: Simplify the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx] using symmetry.
sections.readable_text: Simplify the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx] using symmetry.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall the following:

  • a function [MATH: f(x)] is even if [MATH: f(-x) = f(x)]

  • a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if [MATH: f(-x) = -f(x)]

Moreover, for any even function [MATH: f(x),] the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] is symmetric across the [MATH: y]-axis, so we have [MATH: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2\int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx .]

Notice that [MATH: f(x) = x \sin{x}] is an even function. Indeed, we have

[MATH: f(− x)|= (− x)\sin (− x); = − x(− \sin x); = x\sin x; = f(x).]

So, because [MATH: f(x) = x \sin{x}] is an even function, we have [MATH: \int_{-2}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx = 2 \int_{0}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx.]

items.title: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry?

  1. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx]

  2. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 (e^x+e^{-x}) \, \textrm dx]

  3. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\pi}^{2\pi} \sin(2x) \, \textrm dx]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry?

1. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx]
2. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 (e^x+e^{-x}) \, \textrm dx]
3. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\pi}^{2\pi} \sin(2x) \, \textrm dx]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall the following:

  • a function [MATH: f(x)] is even if [MATH: f(-x) = f(x)]

  • a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if [MATH: f(-x) = -f(x)]

Moreover, for any odd function [MATH: f(x),] the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin, so we have [MATH: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.]

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to [MATH: 0] due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

  • The function [MATH: f(x) = 4x^3] is an odd function: [MATH: f(− x)|= 4(− x)^{3}; = − 4x^{3}; = − f(x)✓] Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that [MATH: \int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx = 0.]

  • The function [MATH: g(x) = e^x+e^{-x}] is not an odd function: [MATH: g(− x)|= e^{(− x)} + e^{− (− x)}; = e^{− x} + e^{x}; = e^{x} + e^{− x}; ≠ − g(x)×]

  • The function [MATH: h(x) = \sin(2x)] is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-a}^a h(x)\,\textrm d x] since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. So, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = A,] what is the value of [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 x\cos x \, \textrm dx?]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = A,] what is the value of [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 x\cos x \, \textrm dx?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall the following:

  • a function [MATH: f(x)] is even if [MATH: f(-x) = f(x)]

  • a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if [MATH: f(-x) = -f(x)]

Moreover, for any odd function [MATH: f(x),] the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin, so we have [MATH: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.]

Notice that [MATH: f(x) = x\cos x] is an odd function. Indeed, we have

[MATH: f(− x)|= (− x)\cos (− x); = − x\cos x; = − (x\cos x); = − f(x).]

So, because [MATH: f(x) = x\cos x] is an odd function, we have [MATH: \int_{-1}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = 0.]

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_{− 1}^{1}x\cos xdx|= 0; ∫_{− 1}^{0}x\cos xdx + ∫_{0}^{1}x\cos xdx|= 0; ∫_{− 1}^{0}x\cos xdx + A|= 0; ∫_{− 1}^{0}x\cos xdx|= − A.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that [MATH: f(x)] is an even function if

Content:
[MATH: f(-x) = f(x).]

Content:
The graph of an even function is always symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/62876bfb7051e069076a858b87da0f43]

Content:
Also recall that [MATH: g(x)] is an odd function if

Content:
[MATH: g(-x) = -g(x).]

Content:
The graph of an odd function always has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. In other words, if we rotate the graph [MATH: 180^\circ] about the origin, the resulting graph looks the same.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b224f670a11fef72c4312785b7530be4]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Integrals of Even Functions

Content:
Let's consider our even function [MATH: f(x)] once more.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/240d86909090a7a6a32b301766952cfa]

Content:
When we have a definite integral of an even function, we can often use symmetry to simplify it.

Content:
From the picture above, we have that

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-a}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx = \int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = A.]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: ∫_{− a}^{a}f(x)dx|= A + A; = 2A; = 2∫_{0}^{a}f(x)dx.]

Content:
To summarize, if [MATH: f(x)] is even, then

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2\int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx .]

Content:
This rule is helpful because definite integrals where one of the integration limits is zero are often easier to evaluate.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Trigonometric Functions

Content:
Throughout this lesson, it's worth remembering that the basic trigonometric functions can be classified as even or odd.

Content:
- [MATH: \cos x] is an even function:
[MATH: \cos(-x) = \cos x]
This function is symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2ac173366c86de65c4992408fae10f5a]

Content:
- [MATH: \sin x] is an odd function:
[MATH: \sin(-x) = -\sin x]
This function has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e69604136ce2de58a8509a2de711721c]

Content:
- [MATH: \tan x] is an odd function:
[MATH: \tan(-x) = -\tan x]
This function has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/79b8293e13131ee488c09354194b9d06]

---

Item 4 — Example: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Even Functions

Example Prompt:
Simplify the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx] using symmetry.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall the following:

- a function [MATH: f(x)] is even if [MATH: f(-x) = f(x)]
- a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if [MATH: f(-x) = -f(x)]

Moreover, for any even function [MATH: f(x),] the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] is symmetric across the [MATH: y]-axis, so we have
[MATH: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2\int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx .]

Notice that [MATH: f(x) = x \sin{x}] is an even function. Indeed, we have

[MATH: f(− x)|= (− x)\sin (− x); = − x(− \sin x); = x\sin x; = f(x).]

So, because [MATH: f(x) = x \sin{x}] is an even function, we have
[MATH: \int_{-2}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx = 2 \int_{0}^2 x \sin{x} \, \textrm dx.]

---

Item 7 — Tutorial: Integrals of Odd Functions

Content:
Let's consider the odd function [MATH: f(x)] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a299dc1f11088a3de4f0f84f009a4fb5]

Content:
From the diagram, we see that
[MATH: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0]

Content:
because the positive and negative areas cancel each other out.

Content:
Furthermore, by the adjacent intervals rule, we can write

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-a}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx + \int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0,]

Content:
which means that

Content:
[MATH: \int_{-a}^0 f(x) \, \textrm dx = - \int_{0}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx.]

---

Item 8 — Example: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero

Example Prompt:
Which of the following integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry?

1. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx]
2. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-2}^2 (e^x+e^{-x}) \, \textrm dx]
3. [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-\pi}^{2\pi} \sin(2x) \, \textrm dx]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall the following:

- a function [MATH: f(x)] is even if [MATH: f(-x) = f(x)]
- a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if [MATH: f(-x) = -f(x)]

Moreover, for any odd function [MATH: f(x),] the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin, so we have
[MATH: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.]

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to [MATH: 0] due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function [MATH: f(x) = 4x^3] is an odd function:
[MATH: f(− x)|= 4(− x)^{3}; = − 4x^{3}; = − f(x)✓]
Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that
[MATH: \int_{-3}^3 4x^3 \, \textrm dx = 0.]

- The function [MATH: g(x) = e^x+e^{-x}] is not an odd function:
[MATH: g(− x)|= e^{(− x)} + e^{− (− x)}; = e^{− x} + e^{x}; = e^{x} + e^{− x}; ≠ − g(x)×]

- The function [MATH: h(x) = \sin(2x)] is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-a}^a h(x)\,\textrm d x] since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. So, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

---

Item 11 — Example: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{0}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = A,] what is the value of [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 x\cos x \, \textrm dx?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall the following:

- a function [MATH: f(x)] is even if [MATH: f(-x) = f(x)]
- a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if [MATH: f(-x) = -f(x)]

Moreover, for any odd function [MATH: f(x),] the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin, so we have
[MATH: \int_{-a}^a f(x) \, \textrm dx = 0.]

Notice that [MATH: f(x) = x\cos x] is an odd function. Indeed, we have

[MATH: f(− x)|= (− x)\cos (− x); = − x\cos x; = − (x\cos x); = − f(x).]

So, because [MATH: f(x) = x\cos x] is an odd function, we have
[MATH: \int_{-1}^{1} x\cos x \, \textrm dx = 0.]

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_{− 1}^{1}x\cos xdx|= 0; ∫_{− 1}^{0}x\cos xdx + ∫_{0}^{1}x\cos xdx|= 0; ∫_{− 1}^{0}x\cos xdx + A|= 0; ∫_{− 1}^{0}x\cos xdx|= − A.]
